articles.title_orig: Iran warns of 'geographically unrestricted response' if US attacks
articles.title_zh: Iran warns of 'geographically unrestricted response' if US attacks
articles.content_orig:
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a warning to the world that “any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Khamenei's threat comes as urgent diplomatic efforts continue to avoid a new all-out Iran war, which would have devastating consequences for the Middle East and beyond, as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran hopes "that there is rationality on the other side to prefer diplomacy to other paths," as "drawing on the experiences of the past two wars, are much stronger than before."
The supreme leader met with Iran’s top military commanders on Saturday, presenting them with directives to prepare for potential new US-Israeli military action, according to the official IRNA news agency.
It follows warnings from the US that its forces could conduct a short but intensive military campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections next week.
The threat of a "geographically unrestricted response" means Iran could look to target Europe as well as Turkey and the South Caucasus in response to a renewed attack.
The description of “any level or type of threat” could indicate that Iran may act pre-eemptively, before a US-Israeli military strike.
State media said that Khamenei - who hasn’t been seen publicly since the Iran war began with US and Israeli strikes in late February - also called for an updated list of potential US and Israeli targets, to include “all kinds of physical and non-physical assets."
Khamenei also said that Iran would decide the duration of any new war.
"Should Iran’s enemies resume military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine when and under what conditions those attacks will end," he said.
Iranian state media reported that in a meeting on Saturday, the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Major General Ahmad Vahidi, together with the Iranian army commander and his chief of staff, briefed the supreme leader on Iran’s military readiness and told him that Iran’s weapons production has increased “seven-fold”.
The commanders report directly to Khamenei and have previously overruled the civilian Iranian leadership fuelling constant speculations as to who makes the decisions in Tehran.
Tehran's threats were reiterated on Sunday by Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia who told Iranian state media that “should a new war erupt, the geography of the conflict will not be confined to the West Asia region,” that "any potential future war could prove significantly longer than past conflicts.”
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a Washington-based think tank, estimated that Khamenei’s threats were “likely part of an Iranian effort to deter the United States and Israel from striking Iran.”
Gulf countries remain "braced for the worst"
While multiple speculations are swirling in the Gulf about the imminence of the war breaking out again versus the state of negotiations, with purported lists of demands from both sides being circulated by medias or whether US negotiators will meet the Iranian ones directly or not, the Gulf nations are bearing the brunt of the months-long state of war, with severe consequences on their economies.
While both the US and Iran have repeatedly pushed previous standoffs to the limit in their attempt to pressure each other into concessions, the Gulf countries continue hoping that a last-minute diplomatic breakthrough of some kind can lead to a peaceful resolution and avert another round of war, especially after the US warned the Gulf that it could launch a new attack on Iran.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told a conference in Bahrain on Sunday that the Gulf states remain "braced for the worst," while hoping that mediation efforts, also led by Qatar, will prevail.
He warned that the Gulf has been blocked in a prolonged state of “no war, no peace,” and that if Washington and Tehran’s “positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.”
The UAE diplomat also decried the Gulf countries’ lack of unity in action as a bloc, stating that “we have not collectively risen to the challenge” and that rebuilding trust with Iran would take an "extremely long time."
Iran recognizes "positive steps" from Washington
While Tehran continues its threats and defiant rhetoric, its foreign minister and its security chief have signalled positive steps in their mediated negotiations with the US via Qatar.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi announced on Saturday evening that Tehran could agree to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in just two days, instead of the previous timeline of seven days.
He said that Iranian diplomats were in Qatar for talks after a Qatari delegation mediated discussions in Tehran over the last few days.
Araghchi last month proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within a week if the US agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions. That was rejected.
In an interview with Qatar-based broadcaster Al Jazeera, Araghchi said that Iran was not planning to meet with US officials but called recent US efforts toward “broader dialogue” a positive step.
Araghchi said a decision on whether negotiations would be direct or indirect would be made “once Washington agrees to Iran’s conditions.”
It comes as the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, said he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance’s proposing negotiations.
Commenting on the letter, Rezaei said “the tone has completely changed” and called it a “very good sign.” Araghchi also called Washington’s attempt to open dialogue a “positive step.”
Rezaei singled out an important change to one of Iran’s conditions: Ships in a reopened Strait of Hormuz would travel on a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman. And “everyone passing through this waterway will do so under Iranian management.”
He said that Iran was now awaiting the latest US response. Separately, Rezaei warned on X that any attack would bring “devastating blows on the aggressor using new weapons.”
Rezaei, who state media this past week said had met with Iran’s supreme leader, also said that there has been no decision to change Iran’s nuclear doctrine, but he noted that some Iranians have questioned whether that should be rethought if Iran is attacked again.
Meanwhile on Sunday, Qatar condemned Friday's attack on one of its LNG tankers in the Gulf, which was hit by "unidentified objects," calling it “a dangerous act that threatens the safety of maritime navigation and the security of global energy supplies”.
Qatar's foreign ministry denounced in a statement “these reckless and irresponsible practices," warning of "serious repercussions that may ensue for the security and stability of the region and the global economy”.

articles.title_orig: Binance to Resume Customer Withdrawals in Phases After Hack
articles.title_zh: Binance to Resume Customer Withdrawals in Phases After Hack
articles.content_orig:
Cryptocurrency exchange says 90% of losses covered as FBI blames North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor
The cryptocurrency exchange Binance has started to allow its customers to withdraw their funds from the platform, as it recovers from a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack.
The exchange was hit by the theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach, but on Sunday announced that it had began a phased reopening after 2pm Singapore time.
The first phase will allow people who hold the ethereum, USDT and USDC tokens on the ethereum blockchain to withdraw their funds, as well as some others held on the BNB Smart Chain blockchain.
The platform said it had replenished 90% of the ⁠amount stolen. The remaining 10% of tokens were less liquid, meaning they ⁠may take ​longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday.
Richard Teng, Binance’s co-chief executive, said separately that the company was “committed to covering the ⁠remaining 10%” and that users would not bear the financial impact of the hack.

It came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
“The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors” were “using to launder these stolen assets”.
Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate.
Binance said it had set aside about $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses. “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.
The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said ​on X.
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.

articles.title_orig: Samsung joins cuff-shaped earbuds trend with $229 Galaxy Buds On
articles.title_zh: Samsung joins cuff-shaped earbuds trend with $229 Galaxy Buds On
articles.content_orig:
It's got a clip-on design to keep them in place.
As competitors like Sony, Bose and Sennheiser reveal their takes on open-ear wireless earbuds, Samsung is taking another stab with the Galaxy Buds On, featuring a clip-on design for a more secure fit. While they don't pack high-level noise cancellation like the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro, the company claims its new Audio Leakage Reduction tech reduces sound leakage by protecting reversed sound waves at the rear of each bud, ostensibly canceling it out. The company says it pulled data from over 119 million ear scans to help the Buds On fit across a range of ear shapes and sizes and have IP54 water resistance.
They're also designed to ensure a low-pressure fit around the ear, something many of us crave from open-ear buds, avoiding the discomfort from typical wireless headphones that form a seal around the ear canal. As mentioned, these aren't Samsung's first open-type design; you might recall the underwhelming Galaxy Buds Live . The more recent (and better) Galaxy Buds 4 launched earlier this year and also have an open-type, semi-in-ear profile like recent AirPods.
The Galaxy Buds On pack a new high-efficiency Class-D amplifier designed to balance power consumption and punchy sound. Battery life also looks solid, with an estimated 9.5 hours of music playback on a single charge. With the charging case, that should stretch to 38 hours.
Samsung's newest buds pack three mics and a voice pickup unit (VPU) that detects speech vibrations, which work together to isolate the caller's voice and cut out noise. Algorithms have been trained on a range of ambient sounds, including construction noises and car horns (is that a regular occurrence on your calls?). The Buds On also pack in head-gesture controls: nod or shake your head to accept or decline calls, and even dismiss alarms and notification readouts. The buds will also work with Galaxy smartphone features, including access to Gemini Live, Quick Voice Memo recordings and will connect to Galaxy phones as soon as you open the case.
The Galaxy Buds On will launch in early November 2026 and will be priced at $229.

articles.title_orig: More than 300 arrests at Palestine Action support protest outside US embassy
articles.title_zh: More than 300 arrests at Palestine Action support protest outside US embassy
articles.content_orig:
More than 300 people have been arrested during a protest supporting the banned Palestine Action group outside the US embassy, police have said.
Hundreds of people gathered at Nine Elms in London on Saturday, with many holding signs reading phrases such as: "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action."
The Metropolitan Police said on Sunday that 325 arrests were made. The force added on social media that 320 of them were for "expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act".
At least 4,000 arrests have been made in relation to the group, which was proscribed in July 2025.
The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action's ban under terrorism legislation , after the group's co-founder was granted permission to appeal it.
The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal.
Officers on Saturday made arrests into the evening, taking people to police vans for transfer, to the applause of many protesters, some of whom chanted: "Free, free Palestine."
In some instances, officers had to carry demonstrators who refused to walk.
Retired lawyer Charles Allison - who was taken by police in the afternoon  - had travelled from Cumbria to participate. He said he feared for people's civil liberties, which he said were "being devalued and watered down".
"I hope the Supreme Court justices - they won't necessarily be influenced by it [the protest] - but I hope that they will take a long-term view of what is happening in this country and decide that the proscription was unlawful, as I believe it was," the 75-year-old said.
David Bolden, another protester awaiting arrest called the ban an "absurd law".
Defend Our Juries, which has been co-ordinating a series of protests over the ban, said the number of people detained this weekend took the total over 4,000 arrests since the group was proscribed, calling it "truly dystopian".
According to Home Office figures seen by the BBC, 3,630 arrests were made in the year ending June 2026. Along with the 134 people arrested outside Westminster Magistrates Court earlier this year and those on Saturday brings the total up to 4,089.
The BBC has contacted the Met to confirm any figures it might hold.
Amnesty International UK has criticised the arrests and called for the government to drop the proscription of Palestine Action.
Defend Our Juries called the arrests "unjust" and an assault on free speech.

articles.title_orig: I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth
articles.title_zh: I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth
articles.content_orig:
Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.
The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.
It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”
I gave an update after the first year , showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.
Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.
So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here . Trust me, you’ll want to.
First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.
Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.
Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.
My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.
By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.
We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.
The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.
But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.
And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).
Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.
The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.
I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!
Of course, not everything is perfect.
The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.
The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.
Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video .
The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.
One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.
And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.
There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.
It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.
One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.
To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.
Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.
The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.
The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).
We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.
After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.
Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.
Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.
You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.
Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.
Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.
Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.
And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.
He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.
In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.
It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV , which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more c

articles.title_orig: Why Europe’s kids are revolting The system won’t save them
articles.title_zh: Why Europe’s kids are revolting The system won’t save them
articles.content_orig:
“The young are a minority in every European society.”  (Kenzo Tribouillard/Getty)
“The young are a minority in every European society.”  (Kenzo Tribouillard/Getty)
All over Europe, the young are in revolt. The student protests in France have drawn most of the attention, not least because of the violence into which they descended, with rioting, looting and the torching of public buildings. But in recent weeks young people have also taken to the streets in a string of other countries, in some cases violently — in Italy, Spain, Portugal, Belgium, Greece, Ireland, Germany, Austria and elsewhere. Meanwhile, in Serbia, a student movement that spent two years in the streets has just won a general election, ending Aleksandar Vučić’s long reign.
The triggers may differ — schools in France and Belgium, housing in Spain and Portugal, the cost of living in Italy, corruption and a mixture of the above in Serbia — but the root is the same. These are the protests of a generation that believes it has been robbed of its future. It’s a conclusion that’s hard to argue with. The social contract its parents knew — work hard and you will, at the very least, secure a home, be able to support a family and be better off than those that came before you — has collapsed. For many young Europeans without inherited wealth, adulthood means drifting from one precarious job to the next, earning barely enough to cover the cost of rent and groceries, let alone start a family. That is, if they find work at all. Meanwhile, they have watched the institutions that were supposed to give them a start in life and cushion its blows — schools, universities, health and youth services — wither under austerity and privatization.
There is no doubt that young people have overwhelmingly borne the brunt of the neoliberal policies pursued over the past decades. That neoliberalism has driven inequality to new heights is widely acknowledged; what is less often noticed is that this inequality is increasingly drawn along generational lines. The geopolitical analyst Arnaud Bertrand recently shared some pretty extraordinary statistics on X regarding France: the over-60s — roughly a quarter of the population — hold around 60% of the nation’s wealth. They also receive nearly two-thirds of all social spending by the French government, in the form of pensions that, under the current system, are paid for by younger generations. This continuous bottom-up generational transfer of wealth is even more extraordinary when one considers that the average French retiree now has an income higher than the average worker .
Yet though the protesters often explicitly frame themselves in generational terms — most obviously Germany’s “ Gen Z regelt ” (which roughly translates as “Gen Z’s got this”) — their demands aren’t phrased as claims against the old. This is surely the right approach. Blaming the boomers would be a mistake. They simply had the good fortune to grow up in an era of full employment, affordable housing and decent pensions, and there is nothing scandalous about aging societies spending more on the old. Moreover, much of that wealth is concentrated in the hands of a small minority of boomers; not all older people live a luxurious life, of course. Ultimately, the problem is not that pensions are too high; it is that the young are being denied what their parents took for granted. The generational divide is simply how a decades-long class war from above is experienced by those who came of age after workers had already lost it, and who inherited a political-economic regime built to transfer wealth upwards. In Europe, that regime has been written into the institutional architecture itself — the euro, the Maastricht treaty, the fiscal rules — which systematically favors asset holders over wage earners, and established workers over new entrants.
The mechanisms are well understood. A decade of quantitative easing inflated the property and financial assets held by the old while wages stagnated, locking the young out of home ownership. Labor market reforms — from Italy’s Treu package and Jobs Act to Germany’s Hartz laws and France’s El Khomri law — preserved the security of those already inside while consigning newcomers to a revolving door of temporary and increasingly precarious contracts in the name of “flexibility”. After 2010, austerity fell disproportionately on education, youth services and public investment. Existing pensions were largely shielded, while future ones were quietly cut. As a result, across Europe, government spending on older people has risen, while public investment has been gutted. Then came the pandemic, which cost Gen Z years of schooling, work and social life, followed by a surge in inflation, made worse by an energy shock that Europe’s leaders largely inflicted on themselves.
As if that weren’t enough, the young are now being told to accept further cuts and deteriorating living conditions to make room for rearmament and an open-ended war — for which, it seems, there is always money. Just a few weeks ago, as French police were firing tear gas at teenagers, EU leaders tasked the Commission with finding another €70 billion for Ukraine in 2027, on top of the €45 billion already earmarked. The fiscal rules that were never relaxed for schools or hospitals are being bent for defense, through national escape clauses and joint borrowing for weapons procurement. And the young have noticed. They are told there is no money for their classrooms, while new billions are found for a war with no end in sight — a war that, as conscription returns to the European agenda, they may even be asked to fight. In many countries, young people are starting to explicitly link the cost-of-living crisis with the rearmament drive.
The real question, then, is not why the young are revolting, but why it took them so long. The economic roots of these protests are undeniable. But are they the whole story? Most conservative commentators have focused instead on the presence of second-generation youths of Arab and African background, and on their leading role in the violence and looting, above all in France but also in Italy. For much of the Right, the riots simply confirm what it has been saying for years: that mass immigration has been an unmitigated disaster, filling European cities with a largely Muslim underclass that has no interest in integrating, and that, in the crudest version of this narrative, is cast as bent on destroying the very fabric of Western civilization, in some cases with the help of the “far-Left”. The demands of the overwhelmingly peaceful protests, meanwhile, go largely unheard.
There is an irony here. The populist Right never tires of complaining that a “globalist establishment” has impoverished and deindustrialized Europe. Yet when young people take to the streets, sometimes violently, against that very establishment and the consequences of its policies, it cannot bring itself to believe that they might have genuine grievances. Instead, it instinctively assumes that someone must be pulling the strings: Islamists, Antifa, Mélenchon.
It is, of course, right to distinguish between the peaceful protests demanding economic reform and the rioting and looting that accompanied them. But are they really two entirely separate stories? There is no question that much of the looting, in France as in Italy, had a strong second-generation component drawn from the banlieues and the marginalized peripheries of Italian cities, with little discernible ideology behind it. Nor is there any point denying the costs of mass immigration, from public safety to the pressure on public services. Many of those involved in the violence were clearly acting out of opportunism. And the growth of separate communities of different social and religious backgrounds, often living in conditions of extreme exclusion, is clearly a social time bomb, one that has already done serious damage to social cohesion — and those on the Left who deny this

articles.title_orig: Microsoft AI beats doctors in simulated diagnosis test
articles.title_zh: Microsoft AI beats doctors in simulated diagnosis test
articles.content_orig:
Laura Ingraham examines the impact of artificial intelligence on healthcare, questioning whether AI will replace doctors. A major public hospital system CEO plans to replace radiologists with AI for breast cancer screening, aiming for cost savings. Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News Senior Medical Analyst, advocates for AI as a tool to enhance, not replace, human doctors, stressing the irreplaceable value of personal interaction and physician oversight for diagnoses.
Ever leave a doctor's appointment with more questions than answers? Maybe you've gone through several tests, only to hear that your doctor still isn't sure what's causing your symptoms. That uncertainty can be exhausting, especially when you want answers. Now, Microsoft says its new artificial intelligence system could help doctors solve some of medicine's toughest diagnostic puzzles. And the early numbers are impressive.
In a study published on Oct. 22 in the journal Science, Microsoft's AI diagnostic system correctly identified 83% of complex medical cases, compared with 36% for generalist physicians who could consult reference materials. That's more than twice the accuracy under the study's testing conditions.
However, there's an important catch behind those numbers. The research took place in a simulation, and the doctors weren't specialists working together on difficult cases. Still, the findings raise a fascinating question about how artificial intelligence could change your next visit to the doctor.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI MAY SPOT DEADLY HEART RISK IN A ROUTINE ECG
Microsoft's MAI-DxO system uses multiple AI agents to evaluate symptoms, recommend tests and work toward a diagnosis. (Microsoft AI)
Microsoft calls its technology the MAI Diagnostic Orchestrator, or MAI-DxO. The system uses multiple AI agents that work together much like a panel of doctors discussing a difficult medical case. Instead of jumping to an immediate answer, the AI begins with limited information. It asks follow-up questions and considers which medical tests might help identify the problem. Then, its AI agents challenge one another's conclusions as new information becomes available.
Think about someone who has unexplained fatigue and several unusual lab results. A doctor might consider one possible explanation before ordering additional tests. Microsoft's system can examine multiple possibilities and reconsider its initial assessment as the evidence changes. That approach could prove especially useful when symptoms overlap across different diseases.
According to Microsoft's published findings, researchers evaluated the technology using 304 complex medical cases from The New England Journal of Medicine . These cases often involve unusual illnesses that challenge even experienced physicians. The results were striking. MAI-DxO correctly diagnosed approximately 83% of those cases. Generalist physicians working alone achieved 36% accuracy when they could use reference materials. Without those resources, their accuracy dropped to 22%. Researchers also tested the system using historical emergency department cases. There, the AI achieved approximately 80% accuracy, compared with 47% for the physician comparison group.
Before anyone starts canceling doctor appointments, there's something important to understand about this research. The physicians in the comparison were generalists, including primary care doctors and general internists. They evaluated cases individually, even when they had access to medical reference materials.
However, hospitals typically involve specialists when patients develop particularly difficult medical problems. Those specialists may work together and review additional evidence before reaching a diagnosis. Microsoft did not directly compare its system against teams of medical specialists.
There's another important detail. Microsoft's AI was evaluated across 304 complex cases, while physicians worked through a smaller set of 56 cases held out from the system's development process. That means the headline percentages don't represent two groups completing exactly the same number of cases.
That limits how broadly we can interpret the findings. The researchers also relied on existing medical cases rather than treating patients in real time. While those cases provide a useful challenge, actual medical care can be far more unpredictable.
Patients sometimes struggle to describe symptoms. Medical records may contain gaps, and physical examinations can reveal clues that never appear in a written case summary. The simulation also relied on an AI system to supply information from existing case reports. When certain details weren't available, it could generate plausible responses. That helped researchers create diagnostic conversations, although those interactions cannot fully reproduce the uncertainty doctors encounter with actual patients.
Furthermore, reaching the correct diagnosis represents only part of caring for someone. Doctors must determine the appropriate treatment and understand how individual circumstances affect medical decisions. The study's authors also work for Microsoft, making independent testing especially important before hospitals consider relying on the technology for patient care. For now, Microsoft's results show how well the technology performed under controlled testing conditions. Whether it can deliver similar benefits during everyday patient care remains an open question.
HIDDEN CLUES COULD HELP PREDICT A WOMAN’S BREAST CANCER RISK YEARS IN ADVANCE
Microsoft's research suggests AI could eventually help doctors diagnose difficult medical conditions more accurately while keeping patients involved in their care. (iStock)
You might be wondering how this technology compares with ChatGPT or other AI assistants that already answer medical questions. The underlying AI models play a major role in Microsoft's system. In fact, the researchers tested models developed by OpenAI, Google , Anthropic and other companies.
One finding deserves attention. OpenAI's GPT-5 correctly solved approximately 79% of the complex cases when researchers used a basic prompt without Microsoft's orchestration system. Adding MAI-DxO increased accuracy to approximately 83%. That's an improvement, although the underlying AI model already performed remarkably well.
With the newer GPT-5.5 model, the gains were larger on complex cases. Microsoft's orchestration system raised accuracy from approximately 72% to nearly 87% in that comparison. However, the additional system provided little improvement on emergency department cases using the strongest models. These results suggest that much of the diagnostic capability comes from powerful AI models themselves. Microsoft's approach can improve its performance further, depending on the model and medical problem.
Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO of AI Mustafa Suleyman has described the company's larger ambition as "medical superintelligence." The idea involves developing AI systems capable of eventually exceeding today's strongest medical teams in clinical reasoning and coordination. Microsoft is also collaborating with Mayo Clinic on AI technology that could eventually help clinicians anticipate how a patient's medical condition might develop. Those ambitions extend well beyond the capabilities demonstrated in the current study.

articles.title_orig: Real Chocolate May Become a Luxury Food
articles.title_zh: Real Chocolate May Become a Luxury Food
articles.content_orig:
Two days before Halloween, an unexpected question is circulating online: Is the chocolate in your candy bowl secretly being grown in a laboratory?
Viral posts claim major candy brands have quietly replaced conventional cocoa with chocolate produced from cells grown in tanks. Snickers, Kit Kat, Hershey, Lindt, and other familiar names have been pulled into the conversation.
On October 29, Snopes investigated the rumor and found no credible evidence supporting the alleged secret switch. Several major chocolate companies explicitly rejected the claims, although not every manufacturer responded.
But here's where the story gets interesting.
Lab grown chocolate is real. Major food companies are investing in it, experimental chocolate bars already exist, and one ingredient supplier is targeting a commercial launch before the end of 2026.
The technology isn't necessarily in your Halloween candy. But it could change how chocolate is made sooner than you think.
Despite the viral claims, there's no credible evidence that major candy brands have secretly switched their existing products to cell cultured cocoa.
According to the October 29 Snopes investigation , several companies addressed the rumor directly.
Hershey said it has no active research, development, or commercialization plans involving lab grown cocoa substitutes. The company also addresses the question on its official ingredients page .
Nestlé said it is not developing lab grown chocolate and remains focused on traditional cocoa production.
Lindt & Sprüngli denied using cultivated cocoa in products currently on the market. However, the company acknowledged investing in Food Brewer, a Swiss startup researching cocoa ingredients grown from plant cells.
Mars , which makes Snickers and M&M's, and Ferrero , which owns Kinder, had not responded to Snopes when the investigation was published.
Because not every company supplied a response and the broader claim lacked sufficient verifiable evidence, Snopes left it unrated rather than issuing a definitive false rating.
That distinction matters. Investing in experimental chocolate technology is not the same as secretly putting it in candy bars.
And not every chocolate alternative is lab grown. Some products use ingredients such as sunflower seeds to create cocoa-free substitutes, an entirely different process.
For now, the viral claim of a widespread, undisclosed switch remains unsupported.
The more immediate chocolate story is happening at the checkout counter.
According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics , prices for candy and chewing gum increased 7.7 percent in the 12 months ending September 2026 , compared with 3.7 percent inflation across all consumer goods and services.
That means candy prices rose more than twice as fast as overall inflation.
West Africa produces much of the world's cocoa, particularly in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. Poor growing conditions, crop disease, and disruptions to harvests helped drive cocoa futures above $10,000 per metric ton after years of substantially lower prices.
Although wholesale cocoa prices subsequently retreated, shoppers haven't seen an equivalent reduction at the register.
Chocolate manufacturers often purchase ingredients through contracts arranged months in advance. Production, packaging, transportation, labor, and other costs also influence the final retail price.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics has examined these broader pressures , which help explain why falling cocoa futures don't immediately translate into cheaper Halloween candy.
And that volatility is part of what makes alternative cocoa production attractive.
Instead of depending entirely on cocoa trees, companies are investigating whether they can grow cocoa ingredients in controlled environments.
It sounds like science fiction, but the concept is relatively straightforward.
Traditional chocolate begins with cacao trees. Farmers harvest their pods, remove the beans, ferment them, dry them, and roast them before turning them into chocolate ingredients.
Cell cultured cocoa starts differently.
Scientists take cells from an actual cacao plant and grow them inside controlled vessels called bioreactors, using nutrients that allow those cells to multiply.
The resulting plant material can then be processed into ingredients intended for chocolate production.
One company pursuing the technology is California Cultured, based in West Sacramento.
According to reporting on its partnership with Belgian chocolate supplier Puratos , the company grows cacao cells in nutrient-rich tanks and can harvest the resulting cell material after approximately three to four days.
The harvested material undergoes processing, including fermentation and roasting, to develop chocolate-like characteristics.
The goal is to produce cocoa ingredients without needing to grow and harvest an entire cacao tree for every production cycle.
That could eventually help manufacturers respond to unstable agricultural supplies, weather disruptions, and fluctuating commodity prices.
Whether the process becomes economically competitive at a large scale remains an important question.
Possibly sooner than many consumers expect—but the distinction between a planned launch and a product already being sold matters.
In February 2026, Puratos announced plans to introduce a chocolate product containing cultured cocoa to professional customers in the United States toward the end of 2026.
The product is being developed with California Cultured.
That means its intended first customers are businesses such as professional chocolate makers, bakeries, and food manufacturers—not necessarily consumers shopping for Halloween candy.
The company has announced its target, but that is not confirmation that the commercial rollout has already happened.
Another player, Israeli biotechnology company Celleste Bio, is developing cocoa butter grown from plant cells.
Backed by Mondelēz International, the company has supplied cultivated cocoa butter for experimental chocolate bars. Reporting in April 2026 detailed nearly a dozen prototype milk chocolate bars produced through the collaboration.
Celleste has targeted market readiness in 2027, subject to regulatory and commercial requirements.
So the timeline looks like this:
Already demonstrated: Experimental chocolate bars containing cell cultured cocoa ingredients.
Late 2026 target: Professional chocolate products incorporating cultivated cocoa.
2027 and beyond: Additional commercial development, subject to approvals and successful production scaling.
There is still no confirmed launch date for a mass-market Snickers, Hershey bar, or Kit Kat made with cultivated cocoa.
There's no compelling reason yet to assume it's either.
Cell cultured cocoa comes from actual cacao plant cells, but growing those cells differently doesn't automatically make the finished ingredient nutritionally identical to conventional cocoa.
The nutritional profile may depend on the cells cultivated, processing methods, and the final formulation.
For example, cocoa contains flavanols, plant compounds studied for their potential cardiovascular effects. Whether future cell cultured ingredients consistently deliver comparable amounts will depend on their composition and processing.
Consumers also need to consider everything else inside a chocolate bar.
Sugar, added fats, portion size, and total calories still matter regardless of where the cocoa originated.
A candy bar doesn't become a health food just because its cocoa was produced using biotechnology.
And the reverse is equally important: the term lab grown alone doesn't establish that an ingredient is harmful.
Individual products would need appropriate safety assessment and regulatory compliance, and meaningful nutritional comparisons require actual product data.
For now, there's no reason to assume your favorite candy bar has secretly been replaced with cultivated cocoa.

articles.title_orig: CEO SUNDAY: Avelo Airlines CEO reveals the habit he credits for his success
articles.title_zh: CEO SUNDAY: Avelo Airlines CEO reveals the habit he credits for his success
articles.content_orig:
Avelo Airlines founder and CEO Andrew Levy shares how hard work, vulnerability and personal accountability have shaped his approach to leadership.
Andrew Levy has spent three decades in the airline industry, building a career that has taken him from airline startups to the executive ranks of one of the nation's biggest carriers .
Through it all, the Avelo Airlines founder and CEO says that hard work has remained a constant throughout his career.
"Working really, really hard. That's the truth," Levy told FOX Business.
BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A FAMILY TURNED CRAFT BEER INTO A HOLIDAY TRADITION
Levy began his aviation career at ValuJet Airlines and later became a co-founder of Allegiant Air, where he held several leadership roles, including president. He went on to serve as chief financial officer of United Airlines before launching Avelo in 2021.
The Avelo CEO also pointed to authenticity and a willingness to show vulnerability as lessons that have shaped his leadership.
CEO SUNDAY: ATOMIC WINGS CEO SHARES HIS JOURNEY FROM WALL STREET TO THE RESTAURANT BUSINESS
Avelo Airlines founder and CEO Andrew Levy says hard work is the habit that has had the biggest impact on his success. (Avelo Airlines)
"I think there's two things," Levy said. "I think one is always be genuine to yourself. And the second one is don't be afraid to show vulnerability."
Levy said vulnerability can sometimes be viewed as a "weakness" in leadership, but he sees it differently.
"The best career advice I think I've received is to just not be afraid to be vulnerable and to show your vulnerability," he said.
Asked about one task he refuses to delegate, Levy said he prefers to handle tough conversations himself.
"Giving bad news," he said. "I think that in my role especially, that it's really important to deliver the good, the bad and the ugly, but not hide behind somebody else to do that, but do it myself."
Levy also pushed back on the perception that being a CEO is an "easy" job.
"It's anything but," he said. "It's constant work. It's a constant focus, attention. It consumes your life."
CEO SUNDAY: DENNY’S CEO SHARES THE SIMPLE RULE GUIDING HIS TURNAROUND OF THE ICONIC DINER CHAIN
Before launching Avelo in 2021, Levy was a co-founder and president of Allegiant Air and later served as chief financial officer of United Airlines. (Avelo Airlines)
He said people may see the title and compensation that can come with running a company without recognizing "the challenges and the toll it takes on you and the investment you have to make as a person to actually be in that role."
"I think there's an underappreciation for how hard it is and the responsibilities that you carry in that role," he added.
For those looking to enter the airline industry, Levy said being comfortable with uncertainty and constant change is essential.
"It's dynamic, it's exciting, but it's constant change," he said. "And you have to enjoy that. You have to enjoy some level of chaos."
If he were not running an airline, Levy said he could see himself working at an investment firm or in private equity, where he could learn about different businesses and industries.
"I would be interested in that only because I get to just see lots of different things," he said, pointing to his "itch" for "constantly learning."
Long before reaching the C-suite, Levy said his first jobs involved raking leaves, pulling weeds and mowing lawns — "whatever I could do to make a little bit of money as a kid."
Asked a series of rapid-fire questions, Levy offered a glimpse into his preferences and personality.

He described himself as a "night owl" who does "a lot of work at night" and said he prefers working in the office.
Asked for his least favorite corporate buzzword, Levy pointed to "laser focused."
"It makes no sense," he said, with a laugh.
When asked for one word his team would use to describe him, Levy answered: "Intense."

articles.title_orig: Gen Z protests turn violent in Germany
articles.title_zh: Gen Z protests turn violent in Germany
articles.content_orig:
Cost-of-living protests in Germany turned violent on Saturday evening with police using water cannons to disperse crowds and masked rioters smashed shop windows, as officials warn the day of rallies organized by a youth-led movement was infiltrated by extremist factions.
Saturday’s action across Germany, organized by the ‘Gen Z has got this!’ movement, railed against the high cost of living, underfunding in education, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service . It follows a wave of similar protests which have swept Europe, including significant unrest in France, which saw a third straight weekend of rallies.
Despite organizers calling for the protests to remain peaceful, violence broke out in some German cities, most notably in Frankfurt and Cologne. Police used water cannons while masked protesters smashed shop windows.
Speaking to German tabloid Bild, Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt said that “violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities” hijacked the peaceful protests, without elaborating further.
The interior minister for the state of Hesse, which includes Frankfurt, warned that “around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists” infiltrated the city’s protest as the evening descended into violence and looting.
“It is shameful how this event here in Frankfurt has ended,” Roman Poseck said.
Poseck said he was determined the violence that has rocked France would not be replicated in Germany.
“We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” he said, according to Reuters. “France must not be held up as a model in this regard.”
In Frankfurt, police said Molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency personnel and shop windows were smashed. Officers arrested a suspect and seized two weapons after windows were broken at a gun shop. According to German news magazine Der Spiegel, several people broke into shops in downtown Frankfurt and over 30 people had been temporarily detained in city by the late evening.
Police in Cologne said water cannons were used after some protesters set off fireworks during a march in the city center. “Our measures are directed against troublemakers and violent individuals – not against peaceful participants,” the police said in a statement.
In Hamburg, riot police responded after barriers were set on fire and emergency service workers were attacked. “There has been an increase in incidents of emergency personnel being pelted with pyrotechnics and construction (materials) … our riot police are taking immediate action against this,” the police said.
Berlin police wrote on X that 27 officers in the German capital had sustained minor injuries and just under 60 people had been detained for offenses including property damage, assault, and resistance against emergency forces.
The movement’s organizers have sought to distance themselves from the ensuing violence. “We had no influence on what happened after the demonstrations ended,” a spokesperson from their press team was quoted by Der Spiegel as saying.
Organizers of ‘Gen Z has got this!’ planned the day of action to coincide with Halloween, to maximize turnout and visibility. According to the organization, 120,000 people attended the protests across Germany on Saturday.
“We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us,” the movement states on its website.
Speaking for his reasons for joining the movement, an 18-year-old student protester in Munich told Reuters, “The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us.” In the eastern city of Dresden, demonstrators held placards reading, “The rich want war, the youth want a future!” and “You’ve screwed up – Gen Z will sort it out.”
More nationwide protests from the Yellow Vests movement took place in France on Saturday, in what was billed as the third act of demonstrations, following earlier protests on October 17 and 24.
This time, however, they were more scaled down than before. The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people protested across the country on Saturday, with 70,000 turning up in Paris; a significantly smaller number than the 550,000 who demonstrated on October 17 and the 410,000 who showed up last week.
The French protests were mostly peaceful, except for a few incidents. The Interior Ministry said in a statement that “radical elements at the tail end of the processions” in several cities. including Bordeaux, Toulouse, Rennes, Lille, Nantes, Marseille, and Lyon, “attempted to enter city centers with the intent to cause damage and engage in looting.”
Protests over soaring housing costs also swept Portugal and Italy on Saturday. In the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, thousands marched to demand Portugal’s center-right government withdraw a rental bill they say will worsen the country’s housing crisis.
In Italy, protests largely led by student groups and workers rallied against inflation, stagnant wages and unaffordable housing in cities including Turin, Bologna and Milan.
CNN’s Pierre P Bairin contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Thousands rally in New Delhi to demand India’s election chief resign
articles.title_zh: Thousands rally in New Delhi to demand India’s election chief resign
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets in India’s capital, New Delhi, to demand the resignation of the election chief over changes to voter lists that opposition parties say favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
Indian National Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi led Sunday’s demonstration, the latest in more than a month of protests challenging the revision of electoral rolls and the conduct of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Opposition parties alleged the exercise, which removed more than 130 million names from voter lists, disproportionately affected Muslims and other minorities considered unlikely to support Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said voters whose names were wrongly removed may register again.
The BJP has accused opposition parties of undermining democracy by challenging legitimate electoral procedures. India’s next general election is due in 2029.
Officials ramped up security measures and announced traffic diversions before demonstrators marched from central New Delhi towards the historic Ramlila Maidan ground.
Hundreds of police, some carrying batons and shields, were deployed around the rally site alongside riot-control vehicles. Demonstrators waved Indian and party flags as opposition leaders travelled in an open-top jeep.
Health Minister Jagat Prakash Nadda dismissed the demonstration as a “carefully orchestrated drama”.
“What is unfolding today at Ramlila Maidan is not an act of respect for democracy,” he told the ANI news agency. “It is a calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy, all in the name of democracy.”
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party have staged near-daily demonstrations since late September, calling for Kumar to step down.
The protests began after Kumar’s two deputies raised concerns about revisions to voter lists, registration procedures and digital systems.
Analysts described the demonstrations and growing support for the opposition as Modi’s most serious political crisis since he took office in 2014.

articles.title_orig: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but history says the stock market's sweetest stretch starts now
articles.title_zh: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but history says the stock market's sweetest stretch starts now
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The AI trade just had its scariest October in years. The rest of the stock market barely noticed.
The biggest AI and chip stocks have shed about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) have each given up roughly $835 billion in market cap, and Intel ( INTC ) lost nearly half its value in October.
Everything else? The other 625 large US stocks in that tally added about $1.3 trillion. And while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped this week, 9 of its 11 sectors rose about 1% or more, something that hadn't happened in any week since at least 1999, by Yahoo Finance calculations.
Jeff Hirsch, editor of the Stock Trader's Almanac , has a name for this: "Octoberphobia." And he's buying the sell-off.
"I did buy some today... this is an opportunity here," Hirsch told Yahoo Finance on Friday . "The damage isn't as bad as the headlines are."
Hirsch also has the calendar on his side. October selloffs like this one often lead into what the Almanac calls the sweet spot of the presidential election cycle , which runs from the fourth quarter of a midterm year through the following June.
From the last October close of a midterm year to the end of the following June, the S&P 500 has risen 19 times out of 19 since 1950 , with a median gain of about 15%. Chip stocks have been 8-for-8 since 1994, with a median gain of about 22%.
The ride wasn't always smooth. Chips fell another 11% or so before turning higher in 2002 and 2018, and eight cycles is a relatively small sample.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) tumbled about 17% in October, yet it's still up more than 50% this year.
On Friday, it dipped as low as $460, below the $464 low from July 29 that marked this summer's bottom. Then it closed at $472, back above that line. That's the look of a bear trap — a breakdown that reverses, catching traders betting on more losses.
Hirsch likes the timing. "Historically, seasonally, it sets up great for this period of time, the best months of the year for semiconductors," he said. His firm placed a new buy in the sector on Friday.
Bulls first need to reclaim about $524, the top of last week's bounce, then the early-October high near $596. Losing the July low would put the February-April range near $370 in play. That's about 21% below Friday's close.
Not everyone is loading up the shopping cart.
BofA's Michael Hartnett said it's "risk-off until global rate hike ends," pointing to 42 central bank rate hikes worldwide over the past six months. The Fed held on Wednesday , but two officials voted to hike. Hartnett's line in the sand for chips is $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF ( SMH ), which closed Friday near $522. On SOXX, that works out to about $469, just above the July low it barely held.
So the bulls' and bears' lines sit almost on top of each other. Hirsch said he'd change his view on a decisive break of the S&P 500's mid-September low near 7,550, less than 1% below Friday's close.
Tuesday's midterm vote comes first. Then November, the S&P 500's best month of the year , gets its turn.

A trip across the U.S.–Canada border could come with a new time difference this winter, even between cities whose clocks usually match.
On November 1, 2026, most of the U.S. and eastern Canada will turn their clocks back one hour, while much of western and central Canada will keep the same time.
This map shows winter time differences across the two countries using the IANA Time Zone Database and provincial and territorial government announcements. Every clock shows the same moment, when it is 4 p.m. in London.
Vancouver and Seattle share the same time through October 31, 2026. The next day, Seattle will turn its clocks back while Vancouver stays put. When it is 8 a.m. in Seattle, it will be 9 a.m. in Vancouver.
British Columbia ended seasonal clock changes for most of the province after its spring adjustment in March 2026. Most of B.C. will keep its summer time through winter, preserving an extra hour of daylight in the late afternoon compared with a return to standard time.
Drag the divider to compare the two maps before and after the November 1 clock change:
Calgary and Edmonton will remain on Regina’s time at 10 a.m., while Denver moves back to 9 a.m. Alberta’s move to permanent time keeps its clocks aligned with Saskatchewan throughout the year. The Northwest Territories is also ending seasonal changes, coordinating with Alberta to preserve shared time for business and health services.
The table below compares local times before and after November 1, using 4 p.m. in London as a common reference point. Time-zone names reflect November 1.
Manitoba is keeping daylight saving time permanently, while Toronto will turn its clocks back. As a result, Winnipeg will share Toronto’s time this winter and be one hour ahead of Chicago. Both Winnipeg and Toronto will show 11 a.m. at the moment illustrated on the map.
Hawaii and most of Arizona already keep the same time throughout the year. The U.S. daylight saving rules exempt both from seasonal clock changes, although the Navajo Nation observes them.
Unlike Canadian provinces, U.S. states cannot adopt permanent daylight saving time without federal authorization. They can stop changing their clocks by keeping standard time, the winter setting, year-round, as Hawaii and most of Arizona already do.
More than 20 U.S. states have passed laws or resolutions supporting permanent daylight saving time . But without a change to federal law, most Americans will continue adjusting their clocks twice a year.
Only 12% of U.S. adults supported changing the clocks twice a year in an October 2025 poll . When asked which time they would prefer year-round, 56% chose daylight saving time, which would mean brighter winter evenings but darker mornings.

Explore the countries with the most islands, led by Sweden, Norway, and Finland, and see how counting rules shape the rankings.
Indonesia and the Philippines are famous for their sprawling tropical archipelagos, but neither tops the list of countries with the most islands.
Instead, Northern Europe dominates the ranking, thanks in part to its intricate coastlines, extensive lake systems, and countless small rocky islands.
This infographic ranks countries by their reported number of islands, using data from national statistical and mapping agencies compiled in Wikipedia’s list of countries by number of islands.
In total, the dataset covers 945,247 islands, although differing national definitions mean this is not a standardized worldwide census.
Sweden ranks first with 267,570 islands, followed by Norway with 239,057 and Finland with 198,146. Together, they account for 704,773 islands, or 74.6% of the total recorded in this ranking.
Scandinavia’s extraordinary island counts are partly the result of its glacial history. During the last Ice Age, glaciers carved and reshaped the landscape, leaving behind countless rocky outcrops, shallow coastal waters, and lake systems as the ice retreated.
Sweden’s Stockholm Archipelago , for example, stretches into the Baltic Sea and contains roughly 30,000 islands, islets, and skerries.
Nearby, Finland’s Archipelago Sea contains tens of thousands of islands, while Norway’s Øygarden Islands, west of Bergen, form a coastal landscape of rocky islands separated by narrow channels.
Canada ranks fourth with 52,455 islands, followed by Chile at 43,471 and the United States at 28,449.
Canada’s reported total refers to coastal islands, excluding the country’s extensive freshwater island geography.
One of its largest island concentrations is the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, which comprises more than 36,000 islands, including Baffin Island , one of the world’s largest.
Farther south, the Alexander Archipelago in southeastern Alaska comprises roughly 1,100 named islands, including Prince of Wales Island and Admiralty Island.
The region is known for its rugged coastline, temperate rainforests, and diverse marine ecosystems.
Meanwhile, Georgian Bay, part of Lake Huron in Ontario, is home to more than 30,000 freshwater islands. This illustrates how Canada’s total island count could be substantially higher under a definition that includes inland islands.
Farther down the ranking, Indonesia has 17,508 islands, followed by Japan with 14,125 and the Philippines with 7,641.
One reason Sweden and Norway rank so highly is that even extremely small islands can qualify. Sweden’s mapping approach recognizes islands as small as 9 square meters, while Norway counts islands around 10 square meters or larger. Both include inland islands.
Japan’s 14,125 figure, meanwhile, is based on naturally formed landmasses with a circumference of at least 100 meters, excluding artificial islands. The count also excludes islands in lakes and rivers, illustrating how different mapping criteria can shape a country’s position in the ranking.
Croatia offers another example: its total of 1,246 combines 79 islands, 525 islets, and 642 rocks or rocks awash, according to research published in Geoadria .
Despite covering just 5% of Earth’s land area, islands are home to an estimated 20% of the world’s bird, reptile, and plant species.
Their geographic isolation allows unique species to evolve, often producing plants and animals found nowhere else. A 2024 study published in Nature found that 21% of the world’s vascular plant species are endemic to islands.
Beyond biodiversity, islands provide important nesting grounds for seabirds and serve as resting points along migration routes.
They are also home to more than 600 million people , supporting distinct cultures and livelihoods closely tied to local ecosystems.

Binance said Sunday it had resumed withdrawals for some major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereal after more than $6 billion in assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
However, the company has offered reassurances it would cover 90% of the losses from the attack using company funds to buy tokens to replenish a large portion of what was stolen.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began on Sunday.
"First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals," the exchange posted on X .
As of 5 a.m. Eastern Time, Binance said it had restored withdrawals for Bitcoin, Ethereal, BNB, XRP, Base, Doge and Optimism, and that it would "continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases as security checks are completed."
The FBI accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.
"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said.
The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s Bid to Stay in Power Will Test His Political Savvy
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s Bid to Stay in Power Will Test His Political Savvy
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his coalition’s parliamentary majority following legislative elections on October 27.
But a bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu also failed to win a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, leaving Israel without a clear path to a new government.
What’s ahead is likely weeks of political wrangling as Israel’s disparate factions weigh possible governing arrangements, including a unity government bringing rival factions together or a minority government reliant on outside support. If they fail to reach an agreement, Israel could head back to the polls.
Here’s what you should know:
The pro-Netanyahu coalition won 53 seats:
A bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats:
Arab-led parties won 19 seats:
That leaves all existing blocs short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, meaning some parties would have to realign or join forces across bloc lines to form a new government.
Israel’s election results must be officially certified and presented to President Isaac Herzog by November 4 .
The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10 .
Herzog must task one incoming Knesset member with forming a new government by November 11 . He is expected to make his decision with input from party leaders, selecting the candidate he believes has the best chance of building a coalition.
The candidate commissioned by Herzog has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible extension of 14 days .
He has not said yet, but the most likely candidates are Netanyahu or former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party received the most votes in the opposition bloc.
According to Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth media, Eisenkot may have an edge over Netanyahu as some Arab-led parties consider endorsing him in a bid to oust Netanyahu.
Herzog, for his part, has urged Israeli politicians to move away from rigid partisan stances and look for “creative solutions” that will lead to a new government and avoid a second round of elections.
Before the election, Herzog said he would do everything he could to spare the country another election cycle, even if that means pressing for a national unity government that brings together rivals Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have previously ruled out partnering with the Arab-led parties .
Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak, however, has said he believes they “can change their mind”, arguing that Netanyahu would do in their position.
“If Netanyahu had a similar problem, he would immediately invite Mansour Abbas”, the leader of Ra’am and “give him the role of a minister of interior”, Barak told France 24 on Friday.
Abbas himself has signalled a willingness to work the opposition camp, saying Eisenkot’s conditions would not pose an obstacle for his party, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
Yousef Jabareen from the Arab-led Joint List has also said that his party is ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”.
“The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.
Even if Arab-led parties do not formally join the opposition’s coalition, they could prop it up from outside by helping it pass a confidence vote in the Knesset.
Raluca Ganea, co-founder of Israeli civil society group Zazim, told Al Jazeera that a coalition between the opposition bloc and the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel “is the only path forward for Israeli democracy as a whole”.
If Herzog’s first candidate fails to form a government within the 42 days, the Israeli president has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.
Even without a coalition commanding at least 61 seats, a candidate could still try to form a minority government by relying on outside support from smaller parties, including Arab-led parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.
If none of these options succeed and deadlock persists, the Knesset would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.
Those elections would have to be called within 90 days.
Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
If the process drags out, that could leave Israel’s longest-serving prime minister in power for months more, even if he ultimately fails to become part of the next governing coalition.
